topic: cutting and raising a green oak frame: layout off one face, mortises, proud pegs and shakes

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: moisture meter cieśli; referent zwyczajny procesowy zakotwiczony poza rozmowa

base: I am cutting an oak frame for a small workshop and the joints fit badly.
An older barn stands across the yard with joints that have held two centuries.
A moisture meter lives in my apron and reads every stick before I cut.
My tenons rock in their mortises and one shoulder stands proud by three millimetres.
Should I pare the shoulders down, or start again with a better layout?
Fix the layout first, because a rocking tenon almost always begins on the line.
Scribe both faces from one reference edge and never measure from the sawn side.
Oak from the mill is rarely square, so the sawn face lies to you.
Pare the shoulders only once the layout is honest on every single timber.
Working from one reference face has made the shoulders sit far more truly.
The tenons still rock slightly, and the mortise walls look bruised inside.
The moisture meter gives twenty eight percent on the timbers I cut last month.
Is that green oak moving on me, or is my chisel work simply poor?
Twenty eight percent is green oak and it will move whatever you do.
Frames were always cut green, so the tradition allows for that movement throughout.
Bruised mortise walls come from levering the chisel rather than cutting the fibres.
Chop from both faces towards the middle and never lever against a wall.
Chopping from both faces has left the walls clean and the tenons snug.
I looked at the older barn again and its pegs stand proud of the posts.
Mine sit flush, which seemed neater when I was trimming them off.
Does it matter whether a peg stands proud or finishes flush with the timber?
It matters a great deal, since a proud peg can be driven again later.
Green oak shrinks around the peg and the joint slackens over the first years.
A flush peg gives you nothing to strike when that slackening finally shows.
Leave a good ten millimetres standing and trim them only after five years.
The frame went up last month and every joint closed as it should.
Fine cracks have opened along the beams, some of them running a metre.
They follow the grain and seem to stop short of every mortise so far.
Should I fill those cracks, or leave them alone as the frame dries?
Leave them alone, because filling traps water and does far more harm than good.
Shakes along the grain are normal in oak and hardly weaken a beam.
Watch only for a crack that runs straight into a mortise or a peg hole.
Such a crack wants a strap, though it is uncommon in a well laid frame.
None of the cracks has reached a mortise and the frame feels solid.
The braces creak loudly, however, when the wind comes hard from the west.
The noise comes from the corner nearest the open gable end of the building.
Is creaking a warning, or just green oak settling into its final shape?
Creaking at an open gable is usually the frame settling rather than failing.
Close the gable in and most of that movement will quieten within a season.
Mark the peg heads with a pencil line and look again in a year.
If a head has crept out, drive it home and the creak will stop.
